findings.supported: Legacy supports[1]; Swift supports[revision2] in checked SDK and runtimes. No revision3 exposed.

findings.candidate: VNTrackObjectRequest revision2; separately new Swift TrackObjectRequest revision2
findings.supported: Legacy supports[1,2]. This is a separate choice from body pose. Current comparison changes only legacy revision, retaining other tracking settings.

findings.finding: New Swift 2D body pose retains ankles and knees but does not add heel/toe landmarks. It does not directly observe toe-to-ball contact.

Apple announced a smaller, faster, more accurate hand model at WWDC25. Joint locations changed. Checked legacy and Swift hand APIs still expose revision1; revision number alone does not identify every OS model update. Current comparison preserves existing hand detector.

Swift DetectHumanBodyPose3DRequest exposes revision1. Depth can help where available, but its coordinates/evidence would require a new validated integration. Not a drop-in fix for current 2D ground logic.

The published session focuses on tap-to-segment, image inputs/tool calling for Foundation Models and Vision on watchOS. It does not announce a body pose revision3. These are not demonstrated real-time juggling contact solutions.

Apple described reference-object tracking on iOS27. It requires prepared 3D reference objects; applicability to small rotating balls and older phones would need separate work. It is not the current VNTrackObjectRequest revision2 experiment.

ARKit offers rear-camera 3D body tracking and foot/toe skeleton joints. A rig joint is not proof of a directly observed toe; tracking confidence and camera integration need separate validation. This is a separate AR session architecture, not a Vision revision switch. No ARKit performance/accuracy test was performed here.

limits: Latest refers to the checked public Apple documentation, installed SDK and reported runtime revisions.
Mac pose coverage is not phone count accuracy.
A higher-confidence joint is not necessarily correctly positioned.
Changing the OS can change model behavior without a new exposed revision enum.
